stem:
A trolley on a track is attached by springs to fixed blocks X and Y, as shown in Fig. 4.1. The track contains many small holes through which air is blown vertically upwards. This results in the trolley resting on a cushion of air rather than being in direct contact with the track.

[[fig:f1]]

The trolley is pulled to one side of its equilibrium position and then released so that it oscillates initially with simple harmonic motion. After a short time, the air blower is switched off. The variation with time *t* of the distance *L* of the trolley from block X is shown in Fig. 4.2.

[[fig:f2]]

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: the initial amplitude of the oscillations

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: the angular frequency *ω* of the oscillations

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: the maximum speed *v*₀, in cm s⁻¹, of the oscillating trolley.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Apart from the quantities in (a), describe what may be deduced from Fig. 4.2 about the motion of the trolley between time *t* = 0 and time *t* = 24 s. No calculations are required.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text:
On Fig. 4.3, sketch the variation with *L* of the velocity *v* of the trolley for its first complete oscillation.

[[fig:f3]]

figures.caption: Fig. 4.1
figures.alt: A trolley rests on an air cushion on a perforated track and is attached by springs to fixed blocks X and Y.

figures.caption: Fig. 4.2
figures.alt: A graph of distance L in centimetres against time t in seconds shows oscillations with decreasing amplitude after about 14 seconds.

figures.caption: Fig. 4.3
figures.alt: A blank gridded graph with L in centimetres on the horizontal axis and v in centimetres per second on the vertical axis.
